narrative: A Kurdish family from Kobani, a town repeatedly attacked by Islamic State, fled to Turkey in late 2014 with tens of thousands of others when the city became a flashpoint. The father, a barber in his forties, his wife in her late twenties, and their two young sons tried to reach relatives abroad, but their sponsorship application was rejected. They made three failed attempts to leave Turkey. On the fourth, in early September 2015, they worked with smugglers in Izmir to reach the coast near Bodrum and then the Greek island of Kos, borrowing around 4,000 euros for the crossing. Before dawn they set out from an isolated beach to evade the coastguard, in a small inflatable boat meant for about eight people but carrying far more. Within minutes high waves hit, the person steering fled, and the boat capsized. The father fought to hold his wife and two sons, swimming between them in the dark, but one by one they were washed away; his wife and both boys drowned, and he was the only survivor. The body of the younger boy, not yet three, washed up on a beach near Bodrum, and the photograph of it became the image that forced the world to confront the crisis. In all, more than a dozen people died in that one short crossing.
